questions.question: The Scaled Agile Framework approach for coordinating multiple Agile teams.
questions.explanation: SAFe provides a structured approach for scaling Agile practices across large enterprises with multiple teams.

questions.question: The Scrum at Scale concept where multiple Scrums coordinate through representatives.
questions.explanation: Scrum of Scrums is a coordination technique where representatives from multiple teams meet to synchronize work.

questions.question: The Extreme Programming practice of having the entire team collaborate on code simultaneously.
questions.explanation: Mob programming involves the whole team working on the same thing, at the same time, in the same space.

questions.question: The Kanban concept of visualizing and optimizing the entire value stream.
questions.explanation: Value Stream Mapping analyzes the flow of materials and information to identify waste and optimize delivery.

questions.question: The metric measuring time from request to delivery in Kanban.
questions.explanation: Lead time measures the total time from when work is requested until it's delivered to the customer.

questions.question: The Crystal methodology's approach to adjusting processes based on team size and criticality.
questions.explanation: Crystal methodologies adapt their practices based on factors like team size, system criticality, and project priorities.

questions.question: The Feature-Driven Development phase where overall model and feature list are created.
questions.explanation: FDD begins with creating a domain object model and identifying features to be built.

questions.question: The Lean principle of delaying decisions until the last responsible moment.
questions.explanation: Deferring commitment keeps options open and makes decisions based on the best available information.

questions.question: The practice of deploying code to production multiple times per day.
questions.explanation: Continuous Deployment automatically releases every change that passes automated tests to production.

questions.question: The Agile chart tracking remaining work against the Sprint goal.
questions.explanation: Burndown charts track remaining work over time, showing if the team is on track to complete Sprint goals.

questions.question: Several Scrum teams must deliver one integrated product from a single Product Backlog, coordinated by a dedicated integration team. Which Scrum scaling framework applies?
questions.explanation: Nexus, created by Scrum.org, scales Scrum for three to nine teams on one product using a shared Product Backlog and a Nexus Integration Team.

questions.question: A government project has a fixed delivery date and fixed budget, but stakeholders agree low-priority features may be dropped if time runs short. Which Agile framework is built around this constraint?
questions.explanation: DSDM fixes time, cost, and quality while flexing features, using MoSCoW prioritization inside fixed timeboxes.

questions.question: In the INVEST criteria for good user stories, what does the letter 'I' stand for?
questions.explanation: INVEST means Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, and Testable; stories should ideally be independent of each other.

questions.question: The correct order of the three non-daily Scrum events within a Sprint, from first to last.
questions.answer: Sprint Planning, Sprint Review, Sprint Retrospective
questions.explanation: A Sprint opens with Sprint Planning, the increment is inspected at the Sprint Review, and the process is improved at the Sprint Retrospective.

questions.question: The XP role of a real user who sits with the team, writes stories, and answers domain questions daily.
questions.explanation: XP requires an on-site customer embedded with the team to define stories, set priorities, and give immediate feedback.

questions.question: In Scrum, the only role with the authority to cancel a Sprint when the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete.
questions.explanation: Only the Product Owner may cancel a Sprint; it happens when the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete, and it is rare in practice.

questions.question: A Scrum team's velocity over its last three Sprints was 30, 34, and 26 story points. Using average velocity, the number of story points it should plan for the next Sprint.
questions.explanation: Average velocity = (30 + 34 + 26) / 3 = 90 / 3 = 30 story points; yesterday's weather says plan to the observed average.

questions.question: In the Scaled Agile Framework, the timebox (typically 8-12 weeks) during which an Agile Release Train delivers incremental value, ending with an Inspect & Adapt event.
questions.explanation: A Program Increment is SAFe's fixed cadence of iterations for an Agile Release Train, closed by Inspect & Adapt.

questions.question: On a Kanban cumulative flow diagram, a band that keeps widening week over week while the bands below it stay thin indicates this.
questions.answer: A bottleneck at that workflow stage
alternatives: A growing queue / bottleneck in that stage
questions.explanation: A widening band means arrivals exceed departures in that stage, so work-in-progress accumulates there - the signature of a bottleneck.

questions.question: The term for the smallest product version that can be released to gain validated learning and deliver value to early adopters.
questions.explanation: An MVP is the smallest releaseable version built to test assumptions and learn from real users, not a full feature set.
